The Euclidean α-profile metric

4-agent discussion (theory P, computation Q, data analysis R, literature S), two rounds · 2026-10-26 · α(T,G) = |T,G| = min #edges deleted from T so that T → G.
Interactive 3D view (PCA axes) → 3D view with graphs as axes → Graph zoo (136 graphs) → Paper draft (PDF) → LaTeX source →

Summary. The profile φ(G) = (α(T,G)/e(T))T gives an exact Euclidean metric E on homomorphism classes.

  • It reverses the homomorphism order. The main principal axis is the height in that order.
  • It reads the clique number ω and the odd girth exactly.
  • It cannot see χ: no finite family of test graphs can. A source-side profile ψ, equal to the FJT quantity 1 − s(T,G), adds χ.
  • Much of the theory is in Engström–Färnqvist–Jonsson–Thapper (2015) under the name "separation".
  • New here: the Euclidean embedding, an ω-strengthening of the clique lower bound, the blindness result, the link to γ, and the computations.

1. Definition

φ(G) = ( wT · α(T,G) / e(T) )T ∈ 𝔉     E(G,H) = ‖φ(G) − φ(H)‖2
  • Test family 𝔉: the 85 cores (all cores on ≤ 8 vertices, plus C9, C11, Petersen, Grötzsch, Icosahedron).
  • Weights: χ-balanced, wT = 1/√Nχ(T), so each chromatic class of tests carries equal total squared weight.
  • G is the target. That is why φ is constant on homomorphism classes: α(2K4,K3) = 2 ≠ 1 = α(K4,K3), but every α(T,·) agrees on 2K4 and K4.
  • EFJT L2.6Order embedding: G → H ⇒ φ(G) ≥ φ(H) coordinatewise. The converse holds when 𝔉 contains a graph equivalent to G (P).

2. Shape of the space

  • One dominant axis. PC1 carries 92% of the variance and is the height ‖φ‖1. It never decreases along any of the 615,167 comparable pairs among the 1276 cores (R).
  • EFJT P2.4Clique coordinates depend only on ω: α(Kn,G) = C(n,2) − t(n, min(n,ω(G))). Moreover supT φT(G) = 1/ω(G) (P).
  • EFJT P2.5Odd-cycle coordinates take only the values 0 and 1/(2k+1), so they read the odd girth exactly. Odd cycles converge to K2.
  • Clusters follow ω, not χ. Nearest neighbours share ω 96% of the time and χ 81% (R).
  • NewBounded tests can't see χ. If every test has ≤ m vertices and G has odd girth > m, then φ(G) = φ(K2) (P). Q's example: the generalized Mycielskian μ5(C11), with 67 vertices and χ = 4, has exactly the profile of K2 on a 12-test basis.

3. Complete graphs, circular cliques and generalized Petersen graphs

The complete graphs form a straight chain K8 → K7 → … → K3 along the main axis, then jump to K2 at the triangle-free end, where the odd cycles accumulate.

Circular cliques: a Farey staircase

The circular cliques Kp/q form a chain in the homomorphism order. It contains the complete graphs Kn/1 and the odd cycles K(2k+1)/k. In profile space this chain is a staircase:

  • 13 of the 24 are themselves test graphs: K2…K8, C5, C7, C9, C11, K7/2 and K8/3.
  • Each of the other 11 lands exactly on the largest circular clique below it whose numerator is ≤ 8. For example, K13/6 lands on K2, K12/5 on C7, K11/4 on K8/3, and K11/3 on K7/2.
  • K10/3 has χ = 4 but the same profile as K3.
  • NewWhy. χc of a graph on ≤ m vertices is a fraction with numerator ≤ m, and X → Kp/q iff χc(X) ≤ p/q (Vince 1988; Zhu 2001). So tests with ≤ m vertices give φ(Kp/q) = φ(K⌊p/q⌋m), where ⌊r⌋m is the largest fraction ≤ r with numerator ≤ m.

Generalized Petersen graphs

Every GP(n,k) with n ≤ 12 lands exactly on one of seven cores: K2, K3, C5, C7, C9, C11 or Petersen. For 11 of them this is not homomorphic equivalence. They are 3-chromatic graphs of odd girth 5 or 7 that do not map to C5 or C7 (checked by exhaustive search), yet no test with ≤ 12 vertices tells them apart from the cycle. This is the blindness result in action.

4. Seeing χ: the source-side profile ψ

  • Why it's needed. φ records what maps into G, while χ is about where G maps to. The naive α(G,T)/e(G) is not class-invariant (K3 vs Kn,n,n).
  • EFJT T2.1, P5.4Definition (P). ψT(G) = max over edge weights of αw(G,T)/‖w‖, which equals 1 − s(T,G) (FJT) and 1 − 1/χT(G).
  • Properties. ψT is class-invariant and order-preserving. ψT(G) = 0 iff G → T, so ψKk(G) > 0 iff χ(G) > k.
  • Lattice operations. ψ(G⊔H) = max. ψ(G×H) ≤ min, and Shitov's counterexample to Hedetniemi shows this can be strict even on the support.
  • Together: φ reads ω and ψ reads χ, so the gap χ − ω is what panel (b) of the summary figure shows.

Related work: Lovász homomorphism vectors (Lovász 1967; Dell–Grohe–Rattan 2018), Langberg–Rabani–Swamy (APPROX 2006), Färnqvist–Jonsson–Thapper (CSR 2009), Borgs et al. (Ann. Math. 2012), and edit distance to monotone properties (Alon–Stav).

6. Recommendations

  • Default metric: all cores as tests with χ-balanced weights. On the 1276 cores it correlates .92 with dist and .83 with d*, merges no pairs, and is very stable (Spearman ρ ≥ .9995 when any one test is removed).
  • Cheap variant: the 85 tests, which gives ρ = .991 with the default but merges about 5% of pairs.
  • Avoid: the 12-test basis alone (only 16 classes on the 1276 cores) and 1/e(T) weights.
  • Good for: a height function on the hom order; exact ω and odd girth; one embedding carrying three distances; a geometric picture of χ − ω (with ψ).
  • Not good for: χ without ψ; compact invariants; graph-ML features on large graphs, where most coordinates are 0.

7. Open questions

  1. openHow does the minimum size of a separating test family grow? For n ≤ 9 it lies in [253, 311].
  2. openIs the closure of the profile space exactly the profiles of countable graphs? Kn → 0, and the Mycielski chain has a non-realised limit.
  3. openDoes the unweighted source-side profile equal the weighted ψ for all G and T?
  4. openIs d* bi-Lipschitz embeddable into ℓ2, or into the profile space?

P · Theorist · round 1
# Agent P (Theorist) — Round 1: the α-profile φ

Notation. φ_T(G) = α(T,G)/e(T) = 1 − mc_G(T)/e(T), where mc_G(T) is the largest number of edges of T that some vertex map V(T)→V(G) sends onto edges. G is the **target**. E₂ = weighted ℓ₂, E_∞ = sup_T |Δφ_T|, δ = test-graph metric, δ_w = FJT max-metric (A7), d_n = max(α(G,H)/e(G), α(H,G)/e(H)).
**Standing fact (F).** φ_T takes values in (1/e(T))ℤ ∩ [0,1]. So for a finite 𝒯 the image is finite. For an infinite 𝒯, convergence in the product topology means every coordinate is eventually constant.
Script: `discussion2/P_check.py`. On both the 85 cores and the 1276 cores (n ≤ 9) it finds 0 failures for P1 (with 𝒯 = all cores), P4 and P5.

## 1. Order structure
**P1 (Theorem, order embedding).**
- (a) G→H implies φ(G) ≥ φ(H) coordinatewise. *Proof:* compose any map T→G with G→H. No preserved edge is lost.
- (b) If 𝒯 contains a graph hom-equivalent to G, then φ(G) ≥ φ(H) implies G→H. *Proof:* φ_G(H) ≤ φ_G(G) = 0.
- So if 𝒯 contains every connected core, G→H ⇔ φ(G) ≥ φ(H). The homomorphism order embeds **anti-isomorphically** into (ℝ^𝒯, ≤). Connected cores are enough: apply (b) to each component.
- (c) Having only H ∈ 𝒯 is not enough. Take 𝒯 = {K₂}: then φ(K₃) = φ(K₂) = 0, but K₃ ↛ K₂.

**P2 (Theorem + counterexamples, lattice operations).** In the hom order, G⊔H is the join and G×H is the meet. Because φ reverses the order:
- φ(G⊔H) ≤ min(φ(G),φ(H)) and φ(G×H) ≥ max(φ(G),φ(H)).
- Both inequalities can be strict, so **φ is not a lattice map**.
- Exact formula for the union: α(T,G⊔H) = min over partitions (A,B) of V(T) of [e(A,B) + α(T[A],G) + α(T[B],H)].
- *Strict for ⊔:* let G = K₃ and H = Grötzsch (an incomparable pair). Let T be k triangles in a chain, joined by one bridge to a chain of k Grötzsch copies, with chain bridges chosen so they can be preserved. Then α(T,G⊔H) ≤ 1, while α(T,K₃) ≥ k and α(T,Grö) ≥ k. (Here α is superadditive over edge-disjoint subgraphs, and Grötzsch is 4-critical and triangle-free.)
- *Strict for ×:* let T = K₃ ∪ Grötzsch, optionally joined by a bridge. Then α(T,K₃) = α(T,Grö) = 1. But K₃×Grö is triangle-free and is not reached by Grötzsch (Grö ↛ K₃), so α(T, K₃×Grö) ≥ 2.
- Hedetniemi in this language: the set U_n = {x ≥ φ(K_n)} is exactly {χ ≤ n} (by P1). U_n is closed under coordinatewise max of the factor profiles but not under the product, by Shitov.

**P3 (Theorem, the meet and join are exact on clique coordinates).** See P4: φ_{K_k} depends only on ω, and ω(G⊔H) = max(ω(G),ω(H)), ω(G×H) = min(ω(G),ω(H)). So φ_{K_k}(G⊔H) = min and φ_{K_k}(G×H) = max.

## 2. Which parameters φ recovers
**P4 (Theorem, clique coordinates).** α(K_k,G) = C(k,2) − t(k, min(k,ω(G))), where t is the Turán number.
*Proof:* the preserved edges form a k-vertex graph that maps to G. It is therefore K_{ω+1}-free, so Turán's theorem applies. A balanced map onto an ω-clique attains the bound.
- Hence φ_{K_k}(G) = 0 iff ω(G) ≥ k, and φ_{K_k}(G) is strictly decreasing in ω for ω < k.
- So φ_{K_k} for any single k > ω determines ω.

**P5 (Theorem, the sup-norm is 1/ω).** For every T, φ_T(G) ≤ φ_T(K_{ω(G)}) ≤ 1/ω(G). The second step uses a uniformly random ω-colouring. Also φ_{K_k}(G) = (k−ω)/(ω(k−1)) + O(1/k) → 1/ω.
So **sup_T φ_T(G) = 1/ω(G)** (cliques never attain it). Consequently E_∞(G,H) ≥ |1/ω(G) − 1/ω(H)|.

**P6 (Theorem, odd girth).** If G has an edge, then φ_{C_{2k+1}}(G) ∈ {0, 1/(2k+1)}, and it is 0 iff og(G) ≤ 2k+1. So og(G) = min{2k+1 : φ_{C_{2k+1}}(G) = 0}. Also φ_T(K₂) = 1 − b(T), where b is the bipartite (max-cut) density, and φ(K₂) is the maximum of φ over all non-edgeless G.

**P7 (Theorem, χ and χ_f are sandwiched).**
- φ(K_{χ(G)}) ≤ φ(G) ≤ φ(K_{ω(G)}). Also φ(G) ≥ φ(K(a,b)) when χ_f = a/b, via the Kneser graph.
- χ(G) = min{n : φ(G) ≥ φ(K_n)} when G ∈ 𝒯.

**P8 (Counterexample: no finite family sees χ).** Let 𝒯 be any family of graphs with at most m vertices. If og(G) > m, then **φ_𝒯(G) = φ_𝒯(K₂)**. *Proof:* the image of the preserved edges has at most m vertices, so it is bipartite and factors through K₂ ⊆ G.
- So χ, χ_f and even bipartiteness are invisible to every finite or bounded-order 𝒯.
- With summable weights, E₂(G,K₂)² ≤ Σ_{|T|>m} w_T → 0 as og(G) → ∞, for any χ.

**P9 (Theorem, Lipschitz relations).**
- (i) d_n(G,H) ≤ E_∞(G,H) ≤ δ(G,H) = δ_w(G,H) ≤ 1. The first inequality needs G,H ∈ 𝒯.
  - Proof of the upper bound: A1 gives φ_T(H) − φ_T(G) ≤ (1−s(H,G))(1−φ_T(G)).
  - Equality E_∞ = δ holds when 𝒯 = all graphs (D: unweighted inf = weighted s).
- (ii) Raw ℓ∞ dominates dist, but on any infinite 𝒯 that is closed under disjoint copies it is +∞ for distinct classes, since α(mG,H) = m·α(G,H). Only normalised coordinates make sense.
- (iii) E_∞ ≤ 1 ≤ d* trivially, and the bound cannot be reversed: d*(K_n,K_m) = |n−m| while E_∞ ≤ 1. More sharply, E_∞(K_n,K_m) ≤ 1/min(n,m), so (K_n) is **δ-Cauchy**. E is therefore a "high-χ compressing" metric: large χ is far in d* but close in E.
- (iv) E₂ ≤ (Σw)^{1/2} E_∞. The reverse fails: take G_k of girth > k with b(G_k) → 1/2. Then E₂(G_k,K₂) → 0, while δ(G_k,K₂) ≥ φ_{G_k}(K₂) → 1/2.

## 3. Infinite families
**P10 (Theorem).** Let 𝒯 ⊇ all connected cores, with w_T > 0 and Σ w_T < ∞.
- E₂ is a **metric on hom-classes** (by P1).
- Weighted ℓ₂ induces the product topology on [0,1]^𝒯, which is compact. So the space is **totally bounded and separable** (it is countable), but **not complete**.
- **Image not closed:** φ(K_n) → 0. The zero vector would mean "T→G for all T", which no finite G satisfies.
- **Mycielski chain:** M_k ⊂ M_{k+1} has φ(M_k) ↓ ψ with ψ ∉ image. If ψ = φ(G), then ψ_G = 0. By (F), φ_G(M_j) = 0 for large j, so G → M_j. Also ψ_{M_{j+1}} = 0, so M_{j+1} → G → M_j, which contradicts χ(M_{j+1}) > χ(M_j).
- **Not convex:** by (F) each coordinate of the closure lies in a finite set, so the closure is totally disconnected (Cantor-like).
- **Limits:** C_{2k+1} → K₂, and more generally og → ∞ gives → φ(K₂) for any χ (P8). Non-isolated points therefore exist.

**P11 (Conjecture).** cl φ(cores) = {φ(X) : X a countable graph}, where φ_T(X) uses maps into the infinite X. Monotone chains give φ(⋃G_k). Proving it for general sequences needs a compactness or ultraproduct argument.

**P12 (Question).** Is (cores, δ) totally bounded? (K_n) and (C_{2k+1}) are δ-Cauchy. An infinite δ-ε-separated family would need s(H_i,H_j) ≤ 1−ε for all i ≠ j.

## 4. Deleting an edge of the target
**P13 (Theorem).** φ(G−e) ≥ φ(G), and
 α(T,G−e) − α(T,G) ≤ min over optimal f of m_e(f) ≤ e(T) − α(T,G),
where m_e(f) is the number of preserved T-edges that f places on e.
- If T → G, then α(T,G−e) ≤ γ(T,G), the concentration parameter, for every e.
- If G is edge-transitive, average over Aut(G): φ_T(G−e) − φ_T(G) ≤ (1−φ_T(G))/e(G) ≤ 1/e(G).

**P14 (Counterexample: no uniform continuity).** Let G = K₃ with a long path attached, and let e be a triangle edge. Then φ_{K₃} jumps from 0 to 1/3, however large e(G) is. For G = K₂ the jump is b(T) ≥ 1/2 in every coordinate. So φ is edge-continuous only in hom-class-sensitive ways. The bound in P13 is the right local statement.
P · Theorist · round 2
# Agent P — Round 2

## 1. A source-side profile that is constant on hom-classes
**Definition.**
 ψ_T(G) = max over probability weights w on E(G) of α_w(G,T),
where α_w(G,T) is the least w-weight of an edge set A with G − A → T. Equivalently, ψ_T(G) = 1 − s(T,G), the FJT separation. Equivalently again, ψ_T(G) = sup over (X,w) with X → G of α_w(X,T)/w(X).

**P15 (Theorem, the three forms agree).** "sup ≥ max" holds by taking X = G.
For "≤": take X → G via h and push w forward to w′ on G. Any partial map G → T pulls back along h, so mc_T(X,w) ≥ mc_T(G,w′), while w(X) = w′(G).
In the same way, any (X,w) can be restricted to its best G-colourable subgraph, which gives s(T,G) = inf over X → G. This is FJT Lemma 6.
- **This is a finite LP:** minimise t subject to Σ_w(preserved by f) ≤ t for all f : V(G) → V(T), with w a probability vector.
- By LP duality, ψ_T(G) = 1 − max over random maps F of min over e of Pr[F preserves e].
- With unweighted X the sup is the same: use D's random blow-ups. The value is attained at X = G when G is edge-transitive.

**P16 (Theorem: monotone, class-invariant, sees χ).**
- (a) G → G′ implies ψ(G) ≤ ψ(G′). The sup runs over a larger set. So ψ is constant on classes and **order-preserving**, while φ is order-reversing.
- (b) ψ_T(G) = 0 iff G → T. Hence **ψ_{K_k}(G) > 0 iff χ(G) > k**, and ψ_{C_{2k+1}}(G) = 0 iff χ_c(G) ≤ 2 + 1/k.
- (c) ψ(G⊔H) = **max**(ψ(G),ψ(H)) exactly. Write X as a union of components; the ratio for X is a mediant of the component ratios, and each connected component maps into G or into H.
  ψ(G×H) ≤ min(ψ(G),ψ(H)). Equality fails at the coordinate K_k for Shitov's pair. So **Hedetniemi is precisely "ψ_{K_k} is min-multiplicative"**.
- (d) ψ_T(G) ≥ α(G,T)/e(G) = φ_G(T), with equality if G is edge-transitive. So R and S's naive ψ is a lower bound, and it is exact for K_n, C_{2k+1}, Petersen and Kneser graphs.

**Closed forms.**
- ψ_{K_k}(K_n) = 1 − t(n,k)/C(n,2) (FJT Lemma 23).
- ψ_{K_k}(G) is sandwiched between the clique and chromatic values: ψ_{K_k}(K_{ω(G)}) ≤ ψ_{K_k}(G) ≤ ψ_{K_k}(K_{χ(G)}) ≤ 1/k.
- ψ_{K_2}(C_{2m+1}) = 1/(2m+1) and ψ_{K_2}(Petersen) = 1/5.
- ψ_{K_2}(G) = 1 − s(K₂,G), which is Šámal's χ_q via χ_q = 1/(1 − d(K₂,G)).
- Beyond these sandwiches, ψ_{K_k} has no closed form in χ: χ_f-type information enters.

**P17 (Theorem: (φ,ψ) is the better embedding).**
- Take G ↛ H. Then φ separates the pair if G ∈ 𝒯, and ψ separates it if H ∈ 𝒯. So (φ,ψ) needs only **one of the two members** in 𝒯, whichever it is.
- With 𝒯 = {K_k} alone, (φ,ψ) reads off **both ω and χ** exactly.
- In R's terms: φ encodes the up-set (what maps into G) and ψ the down-set (what G maps into).
- Cost: each ψ coordinate is an LP over |T|^{|G|} maps, but it needs only Aut(G)-orbit weights.

## 2. Checking S's claims
- **thm:lower_bound with ω(H): correct and strictly stronger.**
  - If G′ ⊆ G maps to H, then G′ contains no K_{ω(H)+1}, so e(G′) ≤ t(n,ω(H)) ≤ t(n,χ(H)). The bound is |G,H| ≥ e(G) − t(|V(G)|, ω(H)).
  - It is **tight for G = K_n and every H** (P4). The paper's χ-version is tight only when t(n,ω) = t(n,χ), for example when H is complete.
  - Example: |K_5,C_5| = 4. The paper's bound gives 10 − 8 = 2, while the ω-bound gives 10 − 6 = 4.
  - The proof in the paper (lines 207–218) is valid, just weak.
- **Hilbert link: correct.** Let p_G(T) = mc_G(T,w)/w(T), which is positive when G has an edge. Then
  log sup p_H/p_G + log sup p_G/p_H = −log s(G,H) − log s(H,G) = d_Hilbert(p_G,p_H).
  - It is a genuine metric (not just a projective one) because p_G(K₂) = 1 normalises every profile.
  - FJT's d = 1 − s(G,H)s(H,G) = 1 − e^{−d_Hilbert}. This is a concave, subadditive transform of d_Hilbert, so its triangle inequality is inherited.
  - Restricting to the coordinates in 𝔉 gives D's d_𝔉, which is still a pseudometric. So S is right.
  - Note: S's p_G is ψ read from the other side, since 1 − p_G(T) = φ_T(G) and s(T,G) = 1 − ψ_T(G). FJT is therefore a single object that has φ and ψ as its coordinate slices.
- **S's Prop P is false for ⊔.** "φ(G⊔H)_T = min for connected T" fails by P2: T is a chain of k triangles and k Grötzsch graphs joined by a bridge, with value ≤ 1 against ≥ k.
- **S's question 2 (connected T with φ(G×H)_T > max) has answer yes.** Take T = K₃ –bridge– Grötzsch. Then α(T,K₃) = α(T,Grö) = 1, and α(T,K₃×Grö) ≥ 2, using superadditivity over edge-disjoint subgraphs.

## 3. Why ≥ 253 tests are needed (Q)
**P18 (Theorem, critical-cover lemma).** Suppose H → G and G − e → H for **every** edge e (G is "H-critical"). Then α(S,H) = α(S,G) for every test S with mc_G(S) < e(G).
*Proof.* An optimal partial map S → G preserves fewer than e(G) edges, so it misses some edge e. Then S − A → G − e → H, which gives ≤. The reverse inequality ≥ comes from H → G.
So a test that separates G from H must hit **every** edge of G. Hence |V(S)| ≥ |V(G)| and e(S) ≥ e(G). If |V(S)| = |V(G)|, then S contains a spanning copy of G.

**Data check** (`P_forced.py`, n ≤ 9): 251 of the 253 forced pairs satisfy, in every case:
- H → G;
- α(G,H) = 1;
- G is H-critical;
- the pair is a **cover** of the core order: no core lies strictly between H and G.

The χ split is (4,4): 149, (5,5): 47, (4,5): 21, (3,4): 19, and so on.
The other 2 are covers with α = 2. These need the obvious generalisation: every optimal map misses some deletion set A with G − A → H.
**Hence forced tests = the tops of critical covers.** Among cores with at most n vertices, G is near-maximal in size, so it is the only test that hits all of its edges. The lower bound therefore grows with the number of critical covers.

These pairs have only **110 distinct lower ends** (K4: 21, K3: 19, …). Each pair is separated by ψ_H (ψ_H(G) ≥ 1/e(G) > 0 = ψ_H(H)). So the 253-forcing argument does not apply to (φ,ψ). This is concrete evidence for P17.
Q · Experimenter · round 1
# Q (computational experimenter): round 1

Notation: φ_F(G) = (α(T,G)/e(T))_{T∈F}; E_F(G,H) = ||φ_F(G) − φ_F(H)||₂. dist = max(α, αᵀ), d* = its shortest-path closure, d_n = edge-normalized dist (matrices from `../discussion/`).
Basis **B12** = {K2, K3, K4, K5, K6, C5, C7, C9, Petersen, Grötzsch, W5, Icosahedron}. α(K2,·) ≡ 0 on any target with an edge, so B12 is effectively 11 tests.
χ-balanced means test weight w_T = 1/√(number of tests with χ(T)), so every χ class carries total squared weight 1.

Scripts: `Q_testfamily.py` (tasks 1 and 3; output in `Q_testfamily_out.md`), `Q_forced.py` (separation bounds), `Q_crate/` (Rust, task 2), `Q_post.py` → `Q_profiles.csv`.

## 1. Test-family design

### Dimension and agreement with the existing distances (correlations are Pearson/Spearman over all pairs)

| targets | family | #tests | eff. dim (PR) | PC1 | #PCs for 99% | E~dist | E~d* | E~d_n | distinct profiles |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 85 cores | all | 85 | 1.19 | 91% | 13 | .76/.82 | .54/.75 | .91/.78 | 85 |
| 85 | all, χ-balanced | 85 | 1.17 | 92% | 6 | **.87/.86** | **.75/.81** | **.96/.82** | 85 |
| 85 | B12 | 12 | 1.33 | 86% | 6 | .81/.86 | .64/.81 | .95/.84 | **15** |
| 85 | B12, χ-balanced | 12 | 1.20 | 91% | 5 | .85/.87 | .72/.81 | .96/.84 | 15 |
| 85 | triangle-free tests only | 11 | 1.34 | 86% | 7 | .53/.50 | .30/.37 | .70/.56 | 13 |
| 1276 cores | all | 1276 | 1.49 | 81% | 54 | .78/.79 | .59/.75 | .85/.66 | 1276 |
| 1276 | all, χ-balanced | 1276 | 1.20 | 91% | 10 | **.92/.86** | **.83/.83** | .92/.70 | 1276 |
| 1276 | B12 | 12 | 1.53 | 80% | 6 | .87/.85 | .78/.83 | .89/.73 | **16** (188,543 pairs at E=0) |
| 1276 | B12, χ-balanced | 12 | 1.29 | 88% | 5 | .90/.85 | .82/.83 | .91/.75 | 16 |
| 1276 | triangle-free tests only | 16 | 1.79 | 72% | 7 | .41/.13 | .19/.08 | .53/.15 | 18 |

In every row the participation ratio is 1.2 to 1.8, so the one-dominant-axis picture does not come from the 74/85 triangle bias. That axis is a "chromatic/clique scale".

χ-balancing makes the agreement with dist and d* clearly better. On the 1276 cores, Pearson E~d* goes from .59 to .83. It also shrinks the spectral tail (54 → 10 PCs for 99%).

B12 gives about the same correlation as all tests at 1% of the cost. However, it collapses the 1276 cores into only 16 classes, so E_{B12} is only a pseudometric.

Spearman agreement between families: E_{B12} vs E_all is .937 (85 cores) and .914 (1276 cores). E_all vs E_all,χ-balanced is .967 and .962.

### Separation: there is no small separating set

- **253** of the 813,450 core pairs (n≤9) are separated by **exactly one** test, and in every case that test is one of the two graphs themselves. Each of these 253 tests is therefore forced, so **any separating family has ≥ 253 tests**.
  - On the 85 cores the same argument forces 37 tests.
- Typical forced pair: a 4-chromatic 8-vertex core T and K3. Here α(T,K3)=1, and α(S,T)=α(S,K3) for every other core S.
- Upper bounds:
  - Greedy over all cores: **321** tests separate all 1276 cores.
  - The 253 forced tests plus a greedy completion: **311**.
  - So the minimum lies in **[253, 311]** (n≤9) and **[37, 42]** (85 cores).
  - The information bound (≤ 8 distinct values per test) would only require 4.
- Restricted candidate pools never separate all cores:

| pool | greedy size | merged pairs left (1276 cores) |
|---|---|---|
| tests with n ≤ 6 | 3 | 327,482 |
| tests with n ≤ 7 | 10 | 94,661 |
| tests with n ≤ 8 | 60 | 40,985 |
| B12 | 7 | 188,543 |
| all non-complete cores | 320 | 6 |

  The 6 merged pairs come from complete targets, which only K_k tests can tell apart.

## 2. Profiles of larger graphs (B12; `Q_profiles.csv`)

Exact branch and bound in `Q_crate`:
- symmetry reduction: one vertex is fixed for vertex-transitive targets, and an arc is fixed for arc-transitive ones;
- a per-vertex lookahead bound and a local-search upper bound;
- checked against the repo `nonhom_param` on all small pairs, with 0 mismatches.

Six cases (Icosahedron into a triangle-free target) hit the 6 s limit with upper bound 10. They are exact by a short argument: Icosahedron has 20 triangles and each edge lies in 2 of them, so at least 10 edges must go; and α(Ico,K2)=10.

Total run time was about 3 minutes.

Each row of the table below gives α(T,G) for T = K2 K3 K4 K5 K6 | C5 C7 C9 | Pet Grö W5 Ico.

| profile class (raw α) | targets with that B12 profile |
|---|---|
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 1 1 1 \| 3 4 3 10 (= K2) | K2, Heawood, C13, C15 |
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 0 0 0 \| 2 3 3 10 (= C5) | C5, dodecahedron, GP(7,2), GP(9,2), GP(11,2), Circ(14;1,4), G(30,.1) |
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 1 0 0 \| 3 4 3 10 | Kneser(7,3) (= C7's profile) |
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 1 1 0 \| 3 4 3 10 | Kneser(9,4) (= C9's profile) |
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 0 0 0 \| 0 3 3 10 | Petersen |
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 0 0 0 \| 0 2 3 10 | Kneser(8,3) (new; no n≤9 core matches) |
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 0 0 0 \| 1 2 3 10 | Circ(13;1,5) |
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 0 0 0 \| 1 1 3 10 | Chvátal, Circ(16;1,3,8) (new) |
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 0 0 0 \| 1 0 3 10 | Grötzsch |
| 0 1 2 4 6 \| 0 0 0 \| 0 0 3 10 | Mycielski M5, Clebsch (new) |
| 0 0 1 2 3 \| 0 \| 0 1 1 3 (= K3) | K3, C11², G(20,.2)#2, G(40,.1) |
| 0 0 1 2 3 \| 0 \| 0 0 1 3 | Paley13, Kneser(6,2) |
| 0 0 1 2 3 \| 0 \| 0 0 0 2 | Kneser(7,2), Paley17 |
| 0 0 1 2 3 \| 0 \| 0 0 0 0 | Icosahedron |
| 0 0 0 1 2 \| 0 … (= K4) | K4, G(20,.2)#1, G(20,.3)#1,#2, G(30,.2) |
| 0 0 0 0 1 \| 0 … (= K5) | G(20,.5)#1,#2 |

- **Heawood: φ = φ(K2), as it must be.** C13 and C15 also equal K2 on B12, because every test has odd girth ≤ 9. The odd graphs K(7,3) and K(9,4) land exactly on C7 and C9. So B12 sees odd girth only up to 9.
- Once G ⊇ K4, the B12 profile depends only on α(K5,G) and α(K6,G). Random graphs therefore fall onto the K4 and K5 points.
- Among triangle-free targets of odd girth 5, the K-, C- and W5/Ico coordinates are all constant. B12 then tells them apart only through the (α(Pet,G), α(Grö,G)) pair, which takes 7 distinct values in this sample.
- Kneser(8,3), Chvátal/Circ(16;1,3,8) and M5/Clebsch have profiles that no n≤9 core has. These are the only new points B12 produces.

## 3. Stability (Spearman ρ between E_F and E_{F±T} over all pairs)

| targets | F | operation | #variants | min ρ | median ρ | most disruptive T |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 85 | B12 | remove one | 12 | .973 | .999 | W5 |
| 85 | B12 | add one core | 73 | .980 | .995 | GQyurg |
| 85 | all | remove one | 85 | .9995 | .9999 | K4 |
| 1276 | B12 | remove one | 12 | .949 | .999 | W5 |
| 1276 | B12 | add one core | 150 (sample) | .968 | .994 | GCZTrW |
| 1276 | all | remove one | 150 (sample) | 1.000 | 1.000 | — |

The large family is extremely stable. The rankings are stable even for B12, but its zero set (which pairs are identified) is not: it changes with every added forced test.

## Takeaways for P/R/S

1. The effective dimension of about 1.2 to 1.5 is intrinsic: it holds for all families tested.
2. χ-balanced weights are the cheap fix that best aligns E with d*: Pearson .83 (vs .59 unweighted) on the 1276 cores.
3. E_F is a metric on cores only if F contains essentially every "near-critical" core. Formally, the minimum separating family is ≥ 253 for n ≤ 9 and grows with n. A finite basis therefore always gives a pseudometric.
4. For large graphs, B12 resolution is bounded by the tests' odd girth (≤ 9) and order (≤ 12). Adding C11, C13 and a χ=5 triangle-free test (M5) would be the next cheap step.

# Q: round 2 (data)

Scripts:
- `Q_crate` (`q_profiles 20 gm`) → `Q_gm.csv`
- `Q_round2.py` → `Q_round2_out.md`
- `Q_3col.py`, a naive 3-colouring check that timed out

Total compute was about 15 min, of which about 10 min was the abandoned colouring check.

## (1a) P8 in data: graphs with χ = 4 that look like K2 or C5

μ_r(C_{2k+1}) is the generalized Mycielskian with r layers. It has odd girth 2k+1 (computed), and χ = 4 for every r by Stiebitz's theorem. My naive 3-colouring search could not finish on 92 vertices, so χ = 4 here rests on the theorem, not on computation.

Each row gives the B12 profile as raw α: K2 K3 K4 K5 K6 | C5 C7 C9 | Pet Grö W5 Ico.

| target | n | m | og | χ | B12 profile | equals φ_B12 of |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| μ₂(C5) | 16 | 30 | 5 | 4 | 0 1 2 4 6 \| 0 0 0 \| 2 3 3 10 | **C5** |
| μ₃(C7) | 29 | 56 | 7 | 4 | 0 1 2 4 6 \| 1 0 0 \| 3 4 3 10 | **C7** |
| μ₄(C9) | 46 | 90 | 9 | 4 | 0 1 2 4 6 \| 1 1 0 \| 3 4 3 10 | **C9** |
| μ₅(C11) | 67 | 132 | 11 | 4 | 0 1 2 4 6 \| 1 1 1 \| 3 4 3 10 | **K2** |
| μ₆(C13) | 92 | 182 | 13 | 4 | 0 1 2 4 6 \| 1 1 1 \| 3 4 3 10 | **K2**: exact for *every* test with ≤ 12 vertices (P8) |
| μ₆(C13) ⊔ C5, also with a bridge | 97 | 187/188 | 5 | 4 | 0 1 2 4 6 \| 0 0 0 \| 2 3 3 10 | **C5**: exact for every test with ≤ 12 vertices |

Notes on the table:
- The Grötzsch and Icosahedron entries on targets of odd girth ≥ 11 timed out at 20 s. They are exact by argument:
  - Icosahedron: on any triangle-free target, 20 triangles with each edge in 2 force α ≥ 10, and α(Ico,K2) = 10.
  - Grötzsch: P8 gives α(Grö, μ₆(C13)) = α(Grö,K2) = 4.
  - For the ⊔C5 graphs the true value is 3, and the solver's upper bound of 4 is not tight. Argument: an image with ≤ 12 vertices meets μ in a bipartite part attached to C5 through at most one cut vertex, so it maps to C5. So α(T, μ⊔C5) = α(T, C5) for |T| ≤ 12.
- **General statement (P8, extended):** if og(G) > m, then φ_𝒯(G ⊔ H) = φ_𝒯(K2 ⊔ H) for every test family 𝒯 of graphs with ≤ m vertices. The same holds with a bridge between G and H.
  - Taking G to be an Erdős graph (large χ, large girth), a fixed finite test family therefore gives **the same profile as K2, or as C5, or as any H, at arbitrary χ**.
  - The smallest witness I have for B12 is μ₅(C11), with 67 vertices and χ = 4. Its profile equals φ(K2) on all 12 basis tests.

## (1b) Source-side ψ(G)_T = max over X→G (X in pool) of α(X,T)/e(X), for T ∈ {K2,…,K5}

ψ depends only on the hom class of G. My χ estimate is the least k with ψ_{K_k}(G) = 0.

| pool of sources X | pool size | χ exact (χ capped at 6) | misses by true χ |
|---|---|---|---|
| all 1276 cores (contains G itself) | 1276 | **1276/1276** | none |
| 85 cores | 85 | 920/1276 | χ=4: 113, χ=5: 236, χ=6: 7 |
| cores with n ≤ 8 | 80 | 906 | 4: 125, 5: 236 |
| cores with n ≤ 7 | 17 | 798 | 4: 196, 5: 272 |
| B12 | 12 | 558 | 4: 423, 5: 286 |
| cores with n ≤ 5 | 5 | 15 | almost all |

- ψ recovers χ **exactly when the pool contains G, or a graph X → G with χ(X) = χ(G)**. That is just χ(G) = max{χ(X) : X → G}, so it is a tautology once G is in the pool.
- With any fixed small pool, ψ only gives a lower bound on χ (each miss underestimates χ).
- This is the source-side mirror of P8: a bounded source pool cannot certify large χ, because the 4-chromatic μ_r(C_{2k+1}) has no small 4-chromatic subgraph.
- The concatenation (φ, ψ) therefore sees χ only through "large" coordinates on both sides.

## (2) Recommended default α-profile metric

Targets: the 1276 cores. Merged pairs are exact counts from integer α.

| tests, weights | E~dist (Pearson/Spearman) | E~d* | E~d_n | merged pairs | ρ vs recommended |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| all 1276, unweighted | .777/.788 | .586/.752 | .847/.655 | 0 | .962 |
| **all 1276, χ-balanced** | **.915/.855** | **.829/.830** | .918/.698 | **0** | 1 |
| all 1276, χ-bal·e(T)^{-1/2} | .902/.854 | .791/.829 | **.922**/.703 | 0 | .999 |
| all 1276, w = 1/e(T) | .740/.752 | .538/.713 | .823/.631 | 0 | .937 |
| 85 tests, χ-balanced | .910/.850 | .822/.830 | .917/.716 | 39,540 | .991 |
| B12, χ-balanced | .899/.849 | .820/.832 | .907/.746 | 188,543 | .935 |

**Recommendation.**
- **Default:** tests = all connected cores up to the size of the targets, weights w_T = 1/√N_{χ(T)}, so each χ class of tests carries equal total squared weight.
  - It is the best on dist and d* among all variants tried.
  - It is a genuine metric on the cores it covers (P1 plus 0 merged pairs).
  - It is stable: dropping any one test gives Spearman ρ ≥ .9995.
- **Cheap version:** the 85 n≤8 tests, χ-balanced.
  - It has ρ = .991 with the default and the same correlations.
  - It is only a pseudometric on n=9: 39,540 merged pairs out of 813k.
  - Leave-one-test-out gives min ρ = .9993.
- **Avoid:** B12 alone (16 classes) and 1/e(T) weighting (it worsens every correlation).
- **Caveat to state:** any finite family gives a pseudometric on larger graphs (separating n ≤ 9 alone needs ≥ 253 tests) and is χ-blind (1a).

## (3) S's closed forms: all confirmed on the 1276 cores

- α(K_k,G) = C(k,2) − t(k, min(k,ω(G))) for k = 2..9: **10,208 / 10,208** entries agree. Here ω is computed from graph6.
- α(C_{2k+1},G) ∈ {0,1}, with 0 iff og(G) ≤ 2k+1, for C5, C7, C9, C11: **5,104 / 5,104** agree. So φ_{C_{2k+1}} ∈ {0, 1/(2k+1)}.
- α(Petersen, C5) = 2, so φ = **2/15** ✓.
- The large targets in `Q_profiles.csv` agree as well. Examples: K-coordinates (1,2,4,6) on all triangle-free targets, and C-coordinates that switch exactly at the odd girth (K(7,3): og 7; K(9,4): og 9).

# Agent R — round 1: what the Euclidean α-profile space lets us see and do

Scripts: `R_analysis.py` (all numbers; full log in `R_analysis_out.txt`), `R_extra.py` (order, segment and cluster checks), `R_figs.py` (figures).
Data: 85-core set (n ≤ 8 plus named graphs; tests are the same 85 cores) and the 1276-core n ≤ 9 set. Invariants (ω, odd girth, χ_f by LP over maximal independent sets, density, triangles per edge) are computed from graph6.

Figures (all in this folder):
- `R_axes.png`: (a) PC1–PC2 with Hasse covers of the hom order; (b) PCA inside ω ≥ 3; (c) PCA inside the triangle-free cores.
- `R_geometry.png`: (a) the K3→K4 segment, with χ-class centroids; (b) each χ-class centroid and the real core nearest to it.
- `R_clusters.png`: (a) Ward dendrogram of the 85 cores; (b) the 1276 cores coloured by Ward k=4.

## 0. A structural fact that reframes PC1: φ is order-reversing (this follows from the definition)
If G → H then α(T,H) ≤ α(T,G) for every T, so **φ(H) ≤ φ(G) coordinatewise**. When H is itself a test, the inequality is strict in coordinate H. Consequences:
- **‖φ‖₁ is a strict linear extension (height function) of the hom order.** Every PC1 loading is ≥ 0 (range 0 to 0.152), and corr(PC1, ‖φ‖₁) = 0.9997. Of the 2966 comparable pairs G→H, **0 violate PC1(G) > PC1(H)**. So the "91% triangle axis" is really **depth in the hom order**. The triangle split shows up only because the hom order has a big gap there: everything with a triangle sits below K3, and K3 is far below the triangle-free cores. See R_axes (a): all 160 Hasse covers point downward.
- **Every core that is also a test is an extreme point of the convex hull of the cloud.** Proof: if φ(G) = Σλ_H φ(H), then coordinate G forces G→H for every H in the support. So φ(H) ≤ φ(G) coordinatewise, and equality of the weighted sum forces φ(H) = φ(G). Checked by LP: 85 of 85 cores are extreme. So "extreme points = cliques and odd cycles" is **false** in full space: every core is extreme. Only the low-dimensional projections have small hulls. In the PC1–PC2 plane the hull is K2, C7, C9, C11, Grötzsch, K6–K8 plus a few n=8 cores.

## 1. Principal axes
All 85 cores (variance 91.4 / 3.1 / 1.3 / 0.8 %):
| PC | best invariant correlates | interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| PC1 | triangle-free +0.94, avg degree −0.77, χ_f −0.69 | hom-order height ≈ ‖φ‖₁ |
| PC2 | ω +0.62, χ_f +0.54, χ +0.53 | clique number (tests K4…K8 load) |
| PC3 | odd girth +0.31 | odd-cycle content: tests C5, Petersen and n=8 triangle-free cores load; separates {K2, C9, C11} from {Grötzsch, …} |
| PC4 | m +0.34, odd girth −0.24 | contrast of K3 versus C5 within the triangle-free group |
| PC5+ | weak (|r| < 0.2) | which particular 4-chromatic 7-vertex cores map in (FQyuo, GCQvRw, …) |

**Removing the triangle effect:**
- *Inside ω ≥ 3 (74 cores; 68 / 14 / 4 %).* PC1 = triangle density (r = −0.85 with triangles per edge; χ_f −0.77). PC2 = clique axis (ω −0.49; tests K4…K8). The picture in R_axes (b) is a **horseshoe**. One arm runs K3, W7 → W5, Icosahedron (ω = 3, increasingly "dense in triangles"). The other arm runs K4 → K5 → … → K8. These are two one-parameter families, not a blob.
- *Inside triangle-free (11 cores).* PC1 (81 %) correlates with **χ_f at r = +0.92**. The order is K2 (2.0), C11 (2.2), C9 (2.25), C7 (2.33), then C5 and Petersen (2.5), the 2.67 cores, and Grötzsch (2.9). The secondary axes separate Petersen from C5 (PC3 is mostly the Petersen test).
- *χ-balanced weights:* PC1 becomes 96.7 % and is still the triangle axis. Reweighting cannot remove it, because it is the order height.
- *After regressing out the ω-class means:* PC1 (52 %) correlates with m (−0.33) and is driven by W5 and the 7-vertex cores; PC2 (12.5 %) is odd girth (+0.38).

**n ≤ 9 (1276 cores; 81 / 7.6 / 2.6 %).** PC1 = triangle density and χ_f (r ≈ −0.8), PC2 = χ/ω (+0.52), PC3/PC4 = triangle-free. The 85-core picture survives.

## 2. Clustering (Ward)
- k=2 is exactly ω=2 versus ω≥3. k=4 gives {ω=2}, {ω=3 near K3, W7}, {ω=3 near W5, Icosahedron}, {ω≥4 cliques}. At k=6 the triangle-free group splits into **{K2, C7, C9, C11}** (bipartite-like, χ_f ≤ 2.33) and **{C5, Petersen, Grötzsch, …}**.
- The nearest neighbour has the same ω in 96 % of cases and the same χ in 81 %. **The space clusters by ω, not by χ.**
- n ≤ 9, Ward k=4: 16 triangle-free | 301 with ω≥4 (all of χ≥5) | **241 = ω=3 and W5 → G (100 %)** | **718 = ω=3 and W5 ↛ G (100 %)**. **Clusters are up-sets of the hom order:** they are defined by which small cores map into G (W5 and W7 have zero α in exactly the 241 group). This is visible only because the space has a centroid-based geometry.
- Most isolated cores (nearest-neighbour E): GEhrvW 0.18, GEhtvW 0.16, GEnb~g 0.15, C7 0.14, Petersen 0.13. The median is 0.07.

## 3. Geometry only Euclidean space allows
- **Centroids (the "average graph").** For χ=5 the centroid is realised: GQz^f{ is 0.056 away, within the class spread of 0.076. For χ=3 (C5 is 0.18 away, spread 0.39) and χ=4 (GCZTuW is 0.17 away, spread 0.27) the centroid is **not** near any core. These classes are not convex blobs: χ=3 mixes K3 with the odd cycles, which sit at opposite ends of PC1. The ω-class centroids are better realised (ω=2 → C5 at 0.11, ω=4 → GQyuv{ at 0.045, ω=5 → K5 at 0.02). This is again consistent with ω being the native coordinate.
- **Straight line K3 → K4 (length 0.68).** Cores sit near the ends: W7 and GCRdrs at t≈0, d=0.07; GEnbv{ and GQjRv{ at t≈1, d=0.05. **Nothing is near the middle.** The nearest core to the midpoint is 0.29 away, which is close to the half-length of 0.34. W5 and the Icosahedron project to t≈0.6 but sit 0.29 off the line. Interpolation therefore exposes a genuine **gap between K3 and K4** that is invisible with dist. Metric betweenness gives the same answer: the best near-between cores have excess ≈ 0.06–0.07 and lie at the ends.
- **Regression φ ~ invariants** (R² over all coordinates): ω one-hot **0.909**; χ one-hot 0.778; χ+ω 0.913; adding odd girth and χ_f reaches 0.937. **φ is about 91 % "ω-class + noise"**; χ adds almost nothing once ω is known.
- **Converse, invariants from φ.** ω is *exactly* readable from single coordinates: ω(G) ≥ k ⇔ φ(G)_{K_k} = 0, and odd girth ≤ 2k+1 ⇔ φ(G)_{C_{2k+1}} = 0. In regression, ω reaches LOO-exact 99 % (85 cores) and 99.8 % (n9). **χ is not linear in φ.** LOO ridge with rounding gets 91 % on the 85 cores and 99.3 % on n9 when only the 85 tests are used. The misses are all cliques (extrapolation), plus Petersen, Grötzsch, C11 and GCrb`o. {χ≤3} is **not linearly separable** with the 85-test features on n9. With all 1276 tests it is separable, but that is trivial because there are as many dimensions as points. χ_f is not recoverable (rounded hits 2 %).
- **Why χ is hidden:** φ uses G as the *target*, so it records what maps **into** G (cliques, odd cycles, W5: the up-set). χ asks what G maps **into**. A "dual" profile ψ(G) = (α(G,T)/e(G))_T would read χ directly via ψ_{K_k} = 0. **Suggestion for P/Q: the concatenation (φ, ψ) should give both ω and χ linearly.**

## Takeaways for the discussion
1. PC1 is not "triangles": it is ‖φ‖₁, a strict height function on the hom order (0 violations).
2. Every test core is an extreme point; this follows from monotonicity.
3. The geometry is organised by ω and by up-sets ("which small cores map in"), not by χ.
4. There is a real empty region between K3 and K4. The χ=3 and χ=4 class averages are not realised by any core.
5. To see χ, add the source-side profile ψ.

# Agent R — round 2

**Scripts and outputs**
- `R_round2.py`: computations; log in `R_round2_out.txt`; numbers cached in `R2_cache.npz`.
- `R_final.py`: draws the summary figure.

**Figure:** `R_final.png`. It has three panels, and only named graphs are labelled:
- (a) the χ-balanced PCA of the 1276 cores;
- (b) ‖φ‖ against ‖ψ‖;
- (c) the B12 PCA, with Q's larger graphs projected onto it.

## (1) χ-balanced weights on the 1276 cores (Q's weights: w_T = 1/√#{tests with χ(T)})
- **Variance explained:** 91.3 / 4.5 / 1.5 %.
- **What PC1 is now:** PC1 correlates −0.93 with χ, −0.92 with ω and −0.91 with χ_f. The triangle indicator drops to 0.53. With the weights, PC1 stops being "contains a triangle" and becomes a **clique/chromatic scale**. The loadings are dominated by K7, K8 and K9, because the singleton χ-classes carry full weight.
- **PC1 is still a hom-order height.** All loadings are ≥ 0, and **0 of the 615,167 pairs G→H** violate PC1(G) > PC1(H). This is P1 again: φ reverses the order, and every non-negative linear functional of φ is monotone along it.
- **What the picture looks like (R_final a):**
  - the clique chain K9 → K4 runs as a diagonal;
  - the χ=5 cloud hangs just after K4;
  - the χ=4 / ω=3 cores form a vertical line from K3/W7 down to W5/Icosahedron (the two up-set clusters from round 1);
  - all triangle-free cores sit in a tight corner: K2 at the top, then C5/Petersen, then Grötzsch.
- **Nearest neighbours:** the nearest neighbour has the same χ in 97.1 % of cases (the same with or without weights) and the same ω in 99.8 %.
- **With B12 only** (12 tests, χ-balanced): 87.7 / 5.9 / 3.9 %. The geometry is qualitatively the same (R_final c).

## (2) The invariant source profile ψ(G)_T = max over X→G of α(X,T)/e(X)
Here X ranges over the 1276 cores and T over the same 1276 tests. This is a lower approximation of P's sup.
- **The fix matters.** ψ is strictly larger than the raw α(G,T)/e(G) in **58.6 %** of the entries. **0 monotonicity failures**: G→H implies ψ(G) ≤ ψ(H), so ψ is order-*preserving* where φ is order-reversing.
- **χ is read exactly from single coordinates:** χ(G) = min{k : ψ(G)_{K_k} = 0}. This holds on all 1276 cores, as it must, since G→K_k makes every source X→G map to K_k.
- **The norm alone sorts χ perfectly on n ≤ 9.** The mean-ψ intervals of consecutive χ-classes do not overlap, and **the top of each class is the clique K_k**. That K_k is the top follows from monotonicity. That the next class starts strictly above it is so far only empirical. So on this data **χ(G) ≤ k ⇔ ‖ψ(G)‖ ≤ ‖ψ(K_k)‖** (R_final b, dashed lines):

| χ | mean ψ | max of class |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | [0.0001, 0.0042] | K3 |
| 4 | [0.0102, 0.1294] | K4 |
| 5 | [0.1345, 0.1778] | |
| 6 | [0.17788, 0.1858] | |

  The 5/6 gap is razor thin, 6·10⁻⁵, so this is a conjecture and not robust.
- **Linear separability of {χ ≤ k} for k = 3, 4, 5** (85 test columns):

| features | separable? |
|---|---|
| φ | no |
| ψ | yes |
| the 2D plane (‖φ‖, ‖ψ‖) | yes |

- **In the ‖φ‖–‖ψ‖ plane** the 1-NN classifier gets χ right 99.1 % of the time. The cloud is an "L" shape:
  - the cliques run up the ψ-axis at φ ≈ 0;
  - the triangle-free cores lie along the φ-axis at ψ ≈ 0;
  - the χ=4 / ω=3 cores fill the corner on an anti-diagonal: Icosahedron and W5 high in ψ and low in φ, K3 and W7 the reverse.
- **Caveat.** ψ is a max over sources with n ≤ 9. For large G it is only a lower bound, and the norm-threshold law may fail once larger sources are allowed. For Mycielski-type G in particular, sources of large odd girth are needed (P8 dualised).

## (3) The five stories the user should know
1. **The main axis is the homomorphism order itself.** PC1 is, to 0.9997 correlation (unweighted), the ℓ1-norm of φ, and it never decreases along G→H: 0 violations in 615k pairs. "Triangle versus triangle-free" (unweighted) or "clique scale" (χ-balanced) are just the largest gaps in that order.
2. **φ sees ω, ψ sees χ, and the χ − ω gap is literally the 2D picture.** ω(G) ≥ k ⇔ φ_{K_k} = 0 (P4), while χ(G) ≤ k ⇔ ψ_{K_k} = 0. Plotting ‖φ‖ against ‖ψ‖ gives an L-shape, and the graphs with χ > ω (Petersen, Grötzsch, W5, Icosahedron, the odd cycles) fill the corner. On n ≤ 9, ‖ψ‖ alone orders the χ-classes with no overlap, with each class topped by its clique.
3. **The space is "lumpy": there is an empty corridor between K3 and K4.** No core lies near the middle of the K3–K4 segment: the nearest is 0.29 away against a half-length of 0.34. The χ=3 and χ=4 "average graphs" are not realised by any core. ω=3, χ=4 graphs such as W5 and Icosahedron sit *off* the line, not between K3 and K4.
4. **Clusters are up-sets: "which small graph maps into G".** On the 1276 cores, Ward clustering splits the 960 ω=3 cores exactly by whether W5 → G (241 versus 718, 100 % pure). The nearest neighbour shares ω in 96–99.8 % of cases.
5. **Big graphs collapse onto small cores in a finite basis** (Q's data, R_final c).
   - Heawood lands on K2, Dodecahedron and GP(k,2) on C5, Kneser(7,3) and Kneser(9,4) on C7 and C9.
   - Dense random G(20, .5) lands on K5, and Paley13 and Kneser(6,2) on one ω=3 point.
   - The only genuinely new points are triangle-free graphs of large χ: Kneser(8,3), Chvátal, Clebsch and Mycielski M5. They sit beyond Grötzsch in the triangle-free corner.
   - This is P8 made visible: a finite test family cannot see large χ hidden behind large odd girth. Every core is still an extreme point of the cloud (round 1).
S · Literature · round 1
# Agent S — Round 1: literature and paper placement for the α-profile

Notation used below:
- α(T,G) = |T,G|, the fewest edges to delete from T so that T maps to G.
- mc_G(T) = e(T) − α(T,G), the size of a largest G-colourable subgraph of T. This is the Max G-Col optimum.
- φ(G)_T = α(T,G)/e(T) ∈ [0,1], and p_G(T) = 1 − φ(G)_T = mc_G(T)/e(T).
- E_w(G,H) = (Σ_T w_T (φ(G)_T − φ(H)_T)²)^{1/2}.

Citation tags:
- **[V]** = checked on the web in this round, or in D_round2.
- **[M]** = from memory, not checked; check before putting it in the paper.

Brute-force sanity checks are in `scratchpad/s_lit/chk2.py`.

## 1. Prior work: is the "α-profile" already known?

**Verdict.** I found **no** paper that defines a vector of normalised max-H-colourable-subgraph values over a family of test graphs, with the target varying, and uses it as an embedding or Euclidean distance. Searches covered:
- "max H-colourable subgraph profile/vector"
- "edge-deletion homomorphism profile"
- "approximate homomorphism indistinguishability"
- "tropical/max-plus homomorphism numbers"
- "homomorphism distance fraction of edges preserved"

The ingredients are all classical, though. Each closest relative below matches one ingredient, so the paper should present φ as a **synthesis** and claim novelty only for that synthesis.

| Line of work | Object | Relation to φ |
|---|---|---|
| **Lovász 1967** [M: "Operations with structures", Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 18 (1967) 321–328]; Lovász, *Large Networks and Graph Limits*, AMS Colloq. Publ. 60 (2012) [M] | hom(F,G) for all F determines G up to isomorphism | φ is the **(max,+) tropicalisation** of the left homomorphism vector (§2, Prop. T). Its zero set {T : φ(G)_T = 0} is the hom-existence profile, which determines the hom-class. |
| **Dell–Grohe–Rattan**, "Lovász meets Weisfeiler and Leman", ICALP 2018, LIPIcs 107, 40:1–40:14, doi:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2018.40, arXiv:1802.08876 [V] https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2018.40 | hom vectors restricted to trees / treewidth ≤ k ⇔ colour refinement / k-WL | A model for "restricted test family ⇒ known equivalence". The analogue for φ is open: which equivalence does φ restricted to a family 𝔉 induce (Q4)? |
| **Grohe**, "word2vec, node2vec, graph2vec, X2vec", PODS 2020, doi:10.1145/3375395.3387641, arXiv:2003.12590 [V] | hom vectors as graph embeddings, "homomorphism indistinguishability" | The ML framing. φ is a new "X2vec" with an optimisation flavour in place of counting. |
| **NT & Maehara**, "Graph Homomorphism Convolution", ICML 2020, PMLR 119:7306–7316, arXiv:2005.01214 [V] https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/nguyen20c.html | hom-count features (bounded-treewidth F) with a universality theorem | Closest ML precedent. A φ-kernel would sit beside it (§3). |
| **BCLSV II**, "Convergent sequences of dense graphs II. Multiway cuts and statistical physics", Ann. of Math. 176 (2012) 151–219, doi:10.4007/annals.2012.176.1.2 [V] | ground-state energies Ê(G,J) = max over q-partitions of Σ J_ij·(edge density between parts), and their cut-continuity ("right convergence ⇔ left convergence") | With J = A_H, Ê(T,A_H)·n² = mc_H(T), so **every coordinate of φ is a ground-state energy of the test T in the "model" G**. The roles are reversed from BCLSV: there the model is fixed and the large graph varies. Here the test varies and the model is the object. Cut-continuity lets φ(G) be evaluated on graphons (Prop. G). |

The additive FJT distance is exactly **Hilbert's projective metric** on the profiles p_G (Prop. H). |
| **Engström–Färnqvist–Jonsson–Thapper**, DMTCS 17:1 (2015) 33–66 [V via D]; arXiv:0904.4600 [V] | s on circular cliques K_{p/q}, links to Šámal's cubical colouring | Source of more closed forms (φ(K_{p/q})_T). |
| **Šámal**, "Cubical coloring — fractional covering by cuts and semidefinite programming", DMTCS 17:2 (2015), arXiv:0911.2589 [V] https://dmtcs.episciences.org/2134 | χ_q(G) from fractional cut covers; FJT state χ_q(H) = 1/(1−d(K2,H)) [V, FJT text] | Gives a "bipartite-density" family of invariants of the same kind. |
| **Langberg–Rabani–Swamy**, "Approximation algorithms for graph homomorphism problems", APPROX 2006, LNCS 4110:176–187, doi:10.1007/11830924_18 [V] | Maximum Graph Homomorphism (MGH): max edges preserved by a map G→H; a (1/2+Ω(1/(|H| log|H|)))-approximation | Proves that **mc_H(T) is the MGH objective**. Cite it for complexity and approximation of the coordinates. |
| **Nakajima–Živný**, "A dichotomy for maximum PCSPs on graphs", arXiv:2406.20069 [V] | MaxPCSP(G,H): given ρ-fraction G-satisfiable, find ρ-fraction H-satisfying | Promise version of comparing two profile coordinates, p_G(T) vs p_H(T). |
| **Edit distance to hereditary properties**: Alon–Stav, "What is the furthest graph from a hereditary property?" RSA 33 (2008) [M for details]; Axenovich–Kézdy–Martin JGT 58 (2008) [V via D]; Balogh–Martin, "Edit distance and its computation", EJC 15 (2008) R20 [V] https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v15i1r20/pdf | ed_𝒫(G) and ed_𝒫(p) | 𝒫_H = {T : T → H} is a **monotone** property, so the edit distance to it is pure deletion. Hence **α(T,H) = ed_{𝒫_H}(T)**, and sup over n-vertex T of α(T,H)/C(n,2) is the Alon–Stav max-distance of 𝒫_H. |
| **Hell–Nešetřil**, *Graphs and Homomorphisms*, OUP 2004 [V via paper]; Welzl, TCS 17 (1982) 29–41 [V via D] | the homomorphism order is a distributive lattice, dense above K2 | φ is an order-embedding of this lattice into ([0,1]^𝔉, ≥) (Prop. O). |
| **Hilbert projective metric**: Hilbert, Math. Ann. 46 (1895) 91–96 [M]; Thompson, Proc. AMS 14 (1963) 438–443 [M]; Lemmens–Nussbaum, *Nonlinear Perron–Frobenius Theory*, CUP 2012 [M] | d_H(x,y) = log max_i(x_i/y_i) + log max_j(y_j/x_j) on positive cones | Identifies FJT's additive metric (Prop. H). |

**Recommended framing sentence.** "The α-profile is the max-plus analogue of Lovász's homomorphism vector. Its coordinates are Max-G-Col values (Langberg–Rabani–Swamy) or ground-state energies (BCLSV) of the test graphs. The Färnqvist–Jonsson–Thapper metric is the Hilbert projective metric on these profiles, and E is the Euclidean counterpart."

## 2. Structural facts and closed forms

### Basic propositions. Proofs are short; they are suitable for the paper.

**Prop. I (well defined on hom-classes; monotone).**
- If G → H, then φ(G)_T ≥ φ(H)_T for every T. Any T − S → G composes to T − S → H.
- Hence G ↔ H implies φ(G) = φ(H).
- *Contrast:* the source side is **not** class-invariant: |2K4,K3| = 2 ≠ |K4,K3| (D_round2).

**Prop. O (order embedding).** Suppose 𝔉 contains the cores of G and H. Then G → H ⇔ φ(H) ≤ φ(G) coordinatewise.
- *Proof of ⇐.* φ(G)_{core G} = 0, so φ(H)_{core G} = 0, i.e. core G → H.
- *Corollary:* E_w (with all w_T > 0) and δ_𝔉 = ‖φ(G)−φ(H)‖_∞ are **genuine metrics on the hom-classes of 𝔉-cores**. This is positivity; symmetry and the triangle inequality come free from the norm.
- *Supporting fact:* the zero pattern of φ(G) is the "Lovász hom-existence vector" {T : T → G}.

**Prop. T (tropicalisation of hom numbers).** Let W_β(G) be the looped complete weighted graph on V(G), with weight e^β on the edges of G and 1 on non-edges and loops. Then

  mc_G(T) = lim_{β→∞} β^{-1} log hom(T, W_β(G)), with 0 ≤ β^{-1}log hom − mc_G(T) ≤ v(T) log v(G)/β.

*Proof.* hom(T,W_β) = Σ_{f: V(T)→V(G)} exp(β·#edges preserved by f). Bound this between the largest term and V(G)^{V(T)} times the largest term.
- *Algorithmic corollary.* The tree-decomposition DP for hom(T,·) works over any commutative semiring. Run it in (max,+) instead of (+,×) to compute mc_G(T) in O(v(T)·v(G)^{tw(T)+1}). This gives a **polynomial-time profile on any bounded-treewidth test family**, exactly as in NT–Maehara and Dell–Grohe–Rattan.

**Prop. F (FJT coordinates).**
- (a) If T is edge-transitive, then φ(G)_T = 1 − s(G,T). This is FJT Lemma 8: s(M,N) = mc_M(N, 1/e(N)) for edge-transitive N.
- (b) In general, s(G,H) = inf_{(T,w)} p_G(T,w)/p_H(T,w). So s is the inf of a coordinate ratio of (weighted) profiles.

**Prop. H (FJT = Hilbert metric on profiles).** Let p_G = 1 − φ(G), indexed by all edge-weighted test graphs. Then

  −log s(G,H) − log s(H,G) = log sup_T p_H(T)/p_G(T) + log sup_T p_G(T)/p_H(T) = d_Hilbert(p_G, p_H).

- max(−log s(G,H), −log s(H,G)) is the Thompson metric.
- Hilbert's metric is projective (zero on proportional vectors). However, p_G(K2) = 1 for every G with an edge, so proportional means equal. The metric property therefore follows from Prop. O, independently of FJT's proof.
- **Consequence for the paper:** δ_𝔉 (ℓ∞), E (ℓ2) and FJT (Hilbert) are three norms/metrics on **one** embedding, G ↦ φ(G). The FJT triangle inequality is the triangle inequality of d_Hilbert.
- *Finite-family version:* d_𝔉 from D_round2 is the Hilbert metric restricted to the coordinates in 𝔉. This explains why it had 0 triangle violations.

**Prop. L (Lipschitz control by the concentration γ).** Let f: T − S → G be optimal, with load μ(f) = max over e ∈ E(G) of |f^{-1}(e)|. Then

  α(T,H) ≤ α(T,G) + μ(f)·α(G,H), so φ(H)_T − φ(G)_T ≤ μ(f)·α(G,H)/e(T).

*Proof.* Delete S, then delete the f-preimages of an optimal S' ⊆ E(G).
- This **links the user's γ parameter to the profile**: γ(T,G), or more precisely the min load over optimal maps, is the local Lipschitz constant of φ under moving the target.
- It is D's load-weighted triangle inequality, now read coordinatewise.

**Prop. P (products and unions of targets).**
- For connected T: φ(G ⊔ H)_T = min(φ(G)_T, φ(H)_T).
- For every T: max(φ(G)_T, φ(H)_T) ≤ φ(G×H)_T ≤ φ(G)_T + φ(H)_T. This uses T' → G×H ⇔ T' → G and T' → H, and deleting S_G ∪ S_H.
- Equality with max holds on cliques and odd cycles, because ω(G×H) = min ω and og(G×H) = max og.
- It fails in general. T = K3 ⊔ Grötzsch, G = K3, H = Grötzsch gives α(T,G×H) = 2 > max(α(T,G), α(T,H)) = 1. Checked: α(Grötzsch,K3) = 1 by brute force.
- **Q:** Is there a *connected* T with φ(G×H)_T > max(φ(G)_T, φ(H)_T)? This is a "profile Hedetniemi" question. Hedetniemi itself (Shitov 2019, Ann. Math. 190 [M]) lives on the *source* side, so it is not this.

### Closed-form coordinates

Recall φ(G)_T = α(T,G)/e(T). Write t(n,r) for the Turán number, ω for clique number, og for odd girth, and T(n,r) for the Turán graph.

| Test T | Target G | α(T,G) | φ(G)_T | Source / status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K_n | **any** G with ω(G) = r | C(n,2) − t(n,r) | 1 − t(n,r)/C(n,2) → 1/r | **New, slightly stronger than the paper.** A subgraph mapping to G is K_{r+1}-free, and blowing up a max clique attains t(n,r). Turán gives the rest. The paper's Thm `thm:KnKm` is the case G = K_m; FJT Lemma 23 gives s(K_r,K_n) = t(n,r)/C(n,2). Brute-force checks: K5→C5: 4, K4→C5: 2, K5→Petersen: 4, K6→Grötzsch: 6. ✓ |
| K_n | C_{2k+1}, k ≥ 2 | C(n,2) − ⌊n²/4⌋ = ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋ | → 1/2 | the row above with r = 2 |
| C_{2k+1} | G non-bipartite, og(G) ≤ 2k+1 | 0 | 0 | C_{2k+1} → C_{og} ⊆ G |
| C_{2k+1} | G bipartite with ≥ 1 edge, or og(G) > 2k+1 | 1 | 1/(2k+1) | path P_{2k+1} → K2. FJT Lemma 18: s(K2,C_k) = s(C_m,C_k) = (k−1)/k for odd k < m. Brute force: C5→C7 gives 1. ✓ |
| C_{2k} or any bipartite T | G with ≥ 1 edge | 0 | 0 | so **bipartite tests carry no information** |
| Petersen P | K2 | 3 | 1/5 | b(P) = 4/5 (Bondy–Locke JGT 10 (1986) [V via D]; FJT p. 900 [V]). Paper `obs:PK2`. |
| Petersen P | C5 | 2 | 2/15 | brute force (chk2.py). P ↛ C5 since χ_c(P) = 3 [M] |
| Petersen P | G ⊇ K3 | 0 | 0 | χ(P) = 3 |
| Dodecahedron | K2 | 6 | 1/5 | brute force; Bondy–Locke extremal [M] |
| Grötzsch (Mycielski of C5) | K3 / C5 | 1 / 3 | 1/20 / 3/20 | brute force |
| Kneser K(2k+1,k) (edge-transitive, odd girth 2k+1) | K2 | ≥ C(2k+1,k)(k+1)/(2(2k+1)) | ≥ 1/(2k+1) | D_round2 averaging argument |
| edge-transitive T | any G | e(T)(1 − s(G,T)) | 1 − s(G,T) | FJT Lemma 8. Imports every FJT/EFJT computation, e.g. wheels: s(K3,W_n) = (2k−3)/(2k−2) for even n [V, FJT Example 9; check indexing] |
| G(n,p), n → ∞ (dense random) | any G with ω(G) = r | — | → 1/r a.s. | Motzkin–Straus (Canad. J. Math. 17 (1965) 533–540 [M]) + quasirandomness. **Dense random tests see only ω.** |
| G(n,c/n) (sparse random) | K2 | — | → 1/2 − P*/√c + o(1/√c) | Dembo–Montanari–Sen, Ann. Probab. 45 (2017) [M]. **Sparse tests see more than ω.** |

**Takeaways from the table.**
- Clique coordinates recover ω(G) exactly. Odd-cycle coordinates recover og(G) exactly.
- Bipartite tests are useless.
- Only "structured" non-bipartite tests carry finer information: Petersen, Kneser, Mycielski, circulants, and the n ≤ 9 cores themselves.
- This is the profile counterpart of D's observation that triangle violations are driven by edge mass.

## 3. Applications

1. **Coordinates for the homomorphism order.** Prop. O makes φ an order-embedding of the hom-lattice of 𝔉-cores into a cube.
   - Agent R can test MDS or PCA on φ to see whether the first principal axes are ω, og and χ-like (cf. the closed forms).
   - Can a "density" result à la Welzl be read off as interpolation of profiles?
2. **CSP approximability, the FJT programme for free.** If Max-M-Col is α-approximable, then Max-N-Col is (1−d)·α-approximable, with d the Hilbert/FJT distance (FJT Lemma 5).
   - Using finite 𝔉 gives *upper* bounds s_𝔉 ≥ s. These are certificates of non-approximability transfer, and computable bounds on FJT distances for the repo's 1276 cores.
   - Concretely, one could tabulate s_𝔉(K2,H) ≈ bipartite-density-type numbers, and so the Goemans–Williamson-transferred ratio 0.878·s(K2,H)... for all cores n ≤ 9.
3. **Graph features / kernels.** The (max,+) DP (Prop. T) gives φ on treewidth-bounded test families in polynomial time.
   - **Caveat:** for large real-world target graphs with ω ≥ 4, every test T with χ(T) ≤ ω maps in, so the profile is near zero. The informative ML object is then the *source* profile ψ(G) = (α(G,H)/e(G))_{H small}: Max-Cut ratio, Max-3-Cut ratio, |G,C5|/e, |G,Petersen|/e, …
   - ψ is Lipschitz under edge edits (1 edit changes α by ≤ 1). It could be compared against hom-count features (NT–Maehara) on TU benchmarks.
   - **Recommend that P/Q also define ψ**, the dual (source-side) profile.
4. **Conjecture testing.**
   - (a) "Profile Hedetniemi" (Prop. P).
   - (b) Odd-girth or circular-chromatic bounds as linear inequalities among coordinates, e.g. φ(G)_{C5} = 0 ⇒ φ(G)_{Petersen} ≤ 2/15? Pentagon/Jaeger-type statements from open_problems/ ask whether specific coordinates vanish (e.g. "P → G for all cubic G of large girth" in the pentagon problem is a statement about a φ(G)_P coordinate).
   - (c) Linear relations: is the convex hull of {φ(G)} over cores polyhedral? This is the analogue of the Razborov / graph-profile region for hom densities.
5. **Graph limits.** By BCLSV cut-continuity [V, abstract], φ(G)_W := 1 − Ê(W; A_G)/t(K2,W) extends φ to graphon tests W (Prop. G). The table rows for dense random graphs are instances of this.

## 4. How to present it in the paper

The place is a new section after `sec:metric` (the m(G,H) section), titled **"The α-profile and metrics on homomorphism classes"**. It also replaces `q:metric`. D_round2 shows q:metric(a) equals |G,H|, and (b) fails under padding.

**Figure suggestion.**
- (i) A heatmap of φ for small cores, with columns = tests (K3, K4, K5, C5, C7, P, Grötzsch, …) and rows = targets.
- (ii) 2-D MDS of E on the 85 cores, coloured by χ, with arrows for the Hasse diagram of →. This shows monotonicity: arrows point "down" in φ.

Agent R/Q's C_mds.png and E_euclid_n8.png from round 1 are near this already.

**Draft LaTeX.**
```latex
\section{The $\alpha$-profile of a graph}\label{sec:profile}

\begin{definition}[$\alpha$-profile]
Let $\mathfrak F$ be a countable family of graphs with at least one edge
(\emph{test graphs}) and $w:\mathfrak F\to(0,\infty)$ with
$\sum_{T}w_T<\infty$. For a graph $G$ the \emph{$\alpha$-profile} is
\[
  \varphi(G)=\Bigl(\tfrac{|T,G|}{|E(T)|}\Bigr)_{T\in\mathfrak F}\in[0,1]^{\mathfrak F},
\]
and the \emph{profile distance} is
$E_w(G,H)=\bigl(\sum_{T}w_T(\varphi(G)_T-\varphi(H)_T)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[invariance and monotonicity]\label{prop:prof_mono}
If $G\to H$ then $\varphi(G)\ge\varphi(H)$ coordinatewise. In particular
$\varphi$ is constant on homomorphism classes.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[order embedding]\label{prop:prof_embed}
If $\mathfrak F$ contains the cores of $G$ and $H$, then
$G\to H \iff \varphi(H)\le\varphi(G)$. Consequently $E_w$ and
$\|\varphi(G)-\varphi(H)\|_\infty$ are metrics on the homomorphism classes
of $\mathfrak F$-cores.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[tropical homomorphism numbers]\label{prop:prof_trop}
Let $W_\beta(G)$ be the weighted looped complete graph on $V(G)$ with weight
$e^\beta$ on $E(G)$ and $1$ elsewhere. Then
\[
 |E(T)|-|T,G| \;=\; \lim_{\beta\to\infty}\tfrac1\beta\log\hom\bigl(T,W_\beta(G)\bigr).
\]
Hence $\varphi(G)_T$ is computable in time $O(|V(T)|\,|V(G)|^{\mathrm{tw}(T)+1})$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[cliques and odd cycles]\label{prop:prof_closed}
For every graph $G$ with $\omega(G)=r\ge 2$ and odd girth $g$,
\[
\varphi(G)_{K_n}=1-\frac{t(n,r)}{\binom n2},\qquad
\varphi(G)_{C_{2k+1}}=\begin{cases}0,& 2k+1\ge g,\\ \frac1{2k+1},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
In particular $\varphi$ determines $\omega(G)$ and the odd girth of $G$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[relation to the FJT metric]\label{prop:prof_fjt}
Let $p_G=1-\varphi(G)$ over all edge-weighted test graphs. Then the
separation of F\"arnqvist--Jonsson--Thapper is
$s(G,H)=\inf_T p_G(T)/p_H(T)$, and
$-\log s(G,H)-\log s(H,G)$ is Hilbert's projective metric between
$p_G$ and $p_H$. For edge-transitive $T$, $\varphi(G)_T=1-s(G,T)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Lipschitz bound via concentration]\label{prop:prof_lip}
If $f:T-S\to G$ is optimal with load $\mu(f)$, then
$|T,H|\le|T,G|+\mu(f)\,|G,H|$.
\end{proposition}
```
Prop. `prof_closed` strengthens `thm:lower_bound`. Replace χ(H) with ω(H) there: |G,H| ≥ e(G) − t(v(G), ω(H)), which is tight for all G = K_n and **all** H. This is a free improvement to the existing paper.

**Open questions for the section.**
1. *(Dimension)* What is the smallest finite 𝔉 such that φ|_𝔉 is injective on cores with ≤ n vertices? Is it much smaller than the set of all such cores?
2. *(Profile Hedetniemi)* Is φ(G×H)_T = max(φ(G)_T, φ(H)_T) for every connected T?
3. *(Profile region)* Describe the closure of {φ(G)} ⊂ [0,1]^𝔉 for 𝔉 = {K3, K4, C5, P}. Which linear inequalities hold (analogue of Razborov's flag-algebra regions)?
4. *(Indistinguishability)* For which families 𝔉 does φ|_𝔉(G) = φ|_𝔉(H) have a logical or algorithmic characterisation, analogous to Dell–Grohe–Rattan for trees and k-WL? Note: for bipartite-free / treewidth-≤2 families this reduces to the odd girth of G.
5. *(Comparison)* Are E_w, δ_𝔉 and d_Hilbert bi-Lipschitz equivalent on cores of bounded size? (The data: corr(d_𝔉, δ_𝔉) = 0.97, D_round2.)
6. *(Limits)* Describe the completion of (hom-classes, E_w) with graphon tests: e.g. K_n → "1/ω profile" sequences.

# Agent S — Round 2: what to keep, what EFJT already has, and the final recommendation

I read P_round1, Q_round1 and R_round1. The paste-ready section is `discussion2/S_section.tex`. It test-compiles cleanly with stub labels and needs no extra packages.

**Sources.** FJT CSR'09 (arXiv:0802.0423) and Engström–Färnqvist–Jonsson–Thapper (EFJT), *DMTCS* 17:1 (2015) 33–66 (https://dmtcs.episciences.org/2118). I extracted the full text of both with pdftotext. Lemma and proposition numbers below are the journal (EFJT) numbering and were checked against that text.

## 1. Much of the profile theory is already in EFJT, in the language of separation

EFJT Definition 1.4: s(M,N) = inf over (G,w) of mc_M(G,w)/mc_N(G,w). Remark 1.5: M→N is not required.

| Our statement | EFJT equivalent | Status |
|---|---|---|
| P1(a) / Prop. I: G→H ⇒ φ(G) ≥ φ(H); class-invariance | Lemma 2.6 (H→N ⇒ s(M,N) ≤ s(M,H); proof: mc_H ≤ mc_N) and Prop. 2.8 (s is well defined on ≡-classes). FJT'09 Lemma 1 / Cor. 2–3. | **Known.** Cite it. |
| P1(b) order embedding (G ∈ 𝔉 ⇒ φ(G) ≥ φ(H) ⇒ G→H) | Implicit in FJT Lemma 4 (positivity of d). Not stated as an embedding. | One-line new observation. Keep. |
| P4: α(K_n,G) = C(n,2) − t(n,ω(G)) | **EFJT Prop. 2.4:** s(H,K_n) = e(T(n,r))/e(K_n) for ω(H) = r, stated with the hypothesis χ(H) ≤ n. The proof does not use that hypothesis. | **Known.** Cite it. The paper's Thm `thm:KnKm` is the special case H = K_m. |
| P6 / odd cycles | **EFJT Prop. 2.5:** s(K2,C_{2k+1}) = s(C_{2m+1},C_{2k+1}) = 2k/(2k+1) | **Known** for targets in the cycle chain. Our general-G version (decided by odd girth) is a trivial extension. |
| Edge-transitive coordinate φ_T(G) = 1 − s(G,T) | **EFJT Thm. 2.1:** s(M,N) = inf over Aut*(N)-invariant w of mc_M(N,w), and = mc_M(N, 1/e(N)) for edge-transitive N. Cor. 2.11: inf over all w on N. | **Known.** |
| P5: sup_T φ_T(G) = 1/ω(G) | Upper bound: Erdős' random r-partition (≥ (1−1/r)e edges) [check: Erdős 1965]. Limit: EFJT Prop. 2.4 as n→∞. EFJT Prop. 2.7 is a different lower bound. | Easy combination; not stated in EFJT. Keep it, short. |
| Hilbert-metric reading of d_FJT | Not in FJT/EFJT; they use d = 1 − s s^T. | **New, but definitional.** State it as a proposition with a one-line proof. |
| P8: bounded tests cannot see χ | Not in EFJT. | **New.** Keep it. |
| P2: not a lattice map | Not in EFJT. | New. Make it a remark with the K3 / Grötzsch example. This also **settles my round-1 "profile Hedetniemi" question negatively**, even for connected T (bridge version). Drop that question. |
| Load / γ Lipschitz bound (P13, my Prop. L) | Not in EFJT. | **New**, and it is the only bridge to the paper's γ. Keep. |
| Q: separating family ≥ 253 for n ≤ 9 | — | Computational remark plus an open question. |
| P10/P11 topology (image not closed, Mycielski chain, closure = countable graphs?) | — | Open question 2. P10's facts go in one sentence. |
| Tropical / (max,+) DP | BCLSV-style. Not in EFJT. | Remark only (computation). |

**Recommended statement list for the section (6 propositions):**
1. Monotonicity and order embedding (cite EFJT 2.6/2.8; the embedding is new). Includes the ‖φ‖₁ height-function corollary (R).
2. Clique and odd-cycle coordinates, reading off ω and odd girth (cite EFJT 2.4/2.5). Plus the **remark improving the paper's `thm:lower_bound` from χ(H) to ω(H)**. Example: |K5,C5| = 4, whereas the χ-bound gives 2.
3. Range: sup φ = 1/ω.
4. Blindness to χ (P8), with Q's ≥ 253 as a computational illustration.
5. Relation to FJT: the edge-transitive coordinate is 1 − s, and the FJT metric is the Hilbert metric on profiles.
6. Moving the target: |T,H| ≤ |T,G| + μ(f)|G,H|, the link to γ.

The lattice failure, the tropical DP and the topology facts become remarks or open questions. Dropped: "profile Hedetniemi" (answered by P2), graphon extension (too far afield), and ML kernel claims (see §3).

## 2. The source-side profile ψ: it is exactly EFJT's separation, read from the other side

P's ψ(G)_T = sup over X→G of α(X,T)/e(X).
- With weighted X, it is **exactly 1 − s(T,G)**. Any (X,w) with X→G has mc_G(X,w) = ‖w‖, so 1 − ψ = inf mc_T(X,w)/‖w‖ ≥ s(T,G). EFJT Thm 2.1 / Cor 2.11 shows the inf over all (X,w) is attained at X = G (which maps to G) with Aut-invariant weights. So
  **ψ^w(G)_T = 1 − s(T,G) = max over w ∈ Ŵ(G) of (1 − mc_T(G,w))**, by EFJT Definition 1.4 + Theorem 2.1.
- Class-invariance in G (and in T) is **EFJT Prop. 2.8**. Monotonicity is Lemma 2.6.
- **EFJT Prop. 5.4:** χ_T(G) = 1/s(T,G), where χ_T(G) is the fractional covering number of G by T-cuts (EFJT Def. 5.2, LP (11)). Hence **ψ^w(G)_T = 1 − 1/χ_T(G)**.
  - For T = K2, χ_{K2} is Šámal's cubical chromatic number, so ψ_{K2}(G) = 1 − 1/χ_q(G).
  - **EFJT Cor. 5.9:** s(K2,G) takes every rational value in (1/2, 1].
- Computation: by Thm 2.1, a coordinate is a small LP over the Aut*(G)-orbits of edges. For edge-transitive G, ψ(G)_T = |G,T|/e(G) exactly.
- **Unweighted version** (sup over simple X→G only). We get ψ ≤ 1 − s(T,G), with equality for edge-transitive G (X = G).
  - Every X→G is a subgraph of a blow-up of G, but blow-ups give only product weights.
  - Equality in general needs D's random-bipartite-block (graphon) argument. Neither FJT nor EFJT states it. This is open question 3 in the section.
- **Recommendation to P.** Define ψ with weights, ψ(G)_T := 1 − s(T,G), cite EFJT, and do **not** present ψ as new.
  - What is new is the pairing (φ, ψ): the target-side column and the source-side row of the separation matrix.
  - Also new is the observation that ψ_{K_k}(G) = 0 ⇔ G → K_k, so ψ sees χ (R's point) while φ sees ω.
  - In this language, d_FJT(G,H) = 1 − (1 − ψ_H(G))(1 − ψ_G(H)) for edge-transitive G,H.

## 3. Final recommendation for the user

**What the profile is good for:**
- **A unifying picture.** One embedding G ↦ φ(G) carries three distances: the ℓ∞ test-graph metric, the Euclidean E, and the FJT metric (Hilbert projective metric).
  - This replaces the failed "is m a metric?" question (`q:metric`) with a clean, true statement: a metric on hom-classes, with an approximation-theoretic meaning through FJT/EFJT Lemma 1.6.
- **Exact readouts.** ω and odd girth come from single coordinates. ‖φ‖₁ is a strict height function of the hom order: R found 0 violations over 2966 comparable pairs.
- **Picturing the hom order.** PCA/MDS figures, clusters that are up-sets, and the empty region between K3 and K4 (R) are good figure material for the computational section.
- **A bridge to γ.** The Lipschitz bound makes the concentration parameter the sensitivity of the profile. This gives the paper's two parameters one storyline.
- **A free improvement to an existing theorem.** |G,H| ≥ e(G) − t(v(G), ω(H)).

**What it is not good for:**
- **χ, χ_f, bipartiteness.** None is visible to any bounded test family (P8). About 91% of the variance is the ω-class (R), and the effective dimension is about 1.2–1.5 (Q).
- **A compact invariant.** Separating the n ≤ 9 cores needs at least 253 tests (Q). Any finite basis gives only a pseudometric.
- **Lattice operations.** φ is not a lattice homomorphism (P2).
- **Graph-ML features on large real graphs.** Targets with ω ≥ 4 swallow every small test. The source side ψ (Max-Cut-type ratios) is the useful feature vector, and ψ is EFJT's separation.
- **Novelty claims.** Clique and odd-cycle values, monotonicity and class invariance are in EFJT. Present the profile as a repackaging plus four new observations: embedding, blindness, the Hilbert form and the γ-Lipschitz bound.

**Three best open questions:**
1. **Separating-family growth σ(n).** We know 253 ≤ σ(9) ≤ 311. Which cores are forced? Is σ(n) of the order of the number of cores?
2. **Closure of the profile space.** Is it exactly the set of profiles of countable graphs (P11)? Is the space of hom-classes totally bounded under ℓ∞ (P12)?
3. **Unweighted equals weighted separation.** Is sup over simple X→G of |X,T|/e(X) = 1 − s(T,G)? A yes would make FJT and ψ weight-free and tie |·,·| directly to EFJT's fractional T-cut covers.
